{{Short description|MRI sequence simulation technique}}
[[File:Epg diagram.png|thumb|The extended phase graph formalism represents the spin vectors along a voxel as a sum of helices with integer numbers of twists.<ref name="pureandsimple"/>]]
In [[magnetic resonance imaging]] and [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] the '''extended phase graph''' (EPG) is a mathematical framework used to track how magnetization evolves in a voxel through a series of radiofrequency (RF) pulses and gradients. While traditional [[bloch equation|Bloch simulations]] track individual spins in the spatial domain, EPG operates in the Fourier domain.<ref name="hennig">{{cite journal|author1= Jürgen K. Hennig|doi=10.1016/0022-2364(88)90128-X|title=Multiecho Imaging Sequences with Low Refocusing Flip Angles |journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance|year=1988 |volume=78 |pages=397–407}}</ref> The magnetization vectors along one dimension of a voxel are stored as [[Fourier series#Definition|Fourier coefficients]]. Each Fourier coefficient represents the weighting of a helix that twists along one dimension of the voxel with an integer number of twists. Performing a weighted sum of all the helices gives the magnetization vectors in the spatial domain. In this representation, a gradient along one dimension of the voxel that causes an integer number of twists simply shifts the index of each Fourier coefficient by that integer, making EPG very computationally efficient at modeling sequences with many RF pulses and gradients. EPG was first proposed by [[Jürgen Hennig]] to model multiecho sequences<ref name="hennig"/> and is now used to model [[magnetic resonance fingerprinting]],<ref name="s668">{{cite journal | last1=Jiang | first1=Yun | last2=Ma | first2=Dan | last3=Seiberlich | first3=Nicole | last4=Gulani | first4=Vikas | last5=Griswold | first5=Mark A. | title=MR fingerprinting using fast imaging with steady state precession (FISP) with spiral readout: MR Fingerprinting with FISP | journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine | volume=74 | issue=6 | date=2015 | pmid=25491018 | pmc=4461545 | doi=10.1002/mrm.25559 | pages=1621–1631 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mrm.25559 | access-date=2026-01-21}}</ref> turbo spin echos,<ref name="w306">{{cite journal | last1=Weigel | first1=Matthias | last2=Hennig | first2=Juergen | title=Contrast behavior and relaxation effects of conventional and hyperecho‐turbo spin echo sequences at 1.5 and 3 T | journal=Magnetic Resonance in Medicine | volume=55 | issue=4 | date=2006 | issn=0740-3194 | doi=10.1002/mrm.20816 | pages=826–835 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mrm.20816 | access-date=2026-01-21| url-access=subscription }}</ref> and other sequences.<ref name="m541">{{cite journal | last1=Sobol | first1=Wlad T. | last2=Gauntt | first2=David M. | title=On the stationary states in gradient echo imaging | journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance Imaging | volume=6 | issue=2 | date=1996 | issn=1053-1807 | doi=10.1002/jmri.1880060220 | pages=384–398 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jmri.1880060220 | access-date=2026-01-21| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Definition ==
In the [[Bloch equations]], within a voxel each spin along the dimension <math>z</math> can be described by a magnetization vector <math>[M_x(z), M_y(z), M_z(z)]^T</math> where every element is real valued.<ref>{{ cite journal | author-link = Felix Bloch | first = F. | last = Bloch | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.70.460 | title = Nuclear Induction | journal = Physical Review | volume = 70 | pages = 4604–73 | year = 1946 |issn=0031-899X}}</ref> But <math>M_x(z)</math> and <math>M_y(z)</math> can also be described by the complex number <math>M_+(z)=M_x(z)+iM_y(z)</math>.<ref name="jaynes">{{cite journal | last=Jaynes | first=E. T. | title=Matrix Treatment of Nuclear Induction | journal=Physical Review | volume=98 | issue=4 | date=1955-05-15 | issn=0031-899X | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.98.1099 | pages=1099–1105 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.98.1099 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref> Using a similarity matrix <math>S</math> we can convert between the real valued basis and the complex transverse magnetization basis:

<math display="block">\begin{align}

&S=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & i & 0 \\ 1 & -i & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}, &\mathbf{m}(z)=\begin{bmatrix} M_+(z) \\ M_-(z) \\ M_z(z) \end{bmatrix}=S \begin{bmatrix} M_x(z) \\ M_y(z) \\ M_z(z) \end{bmatrix}\\

\end{align}</math>

where <math>M_-</math> is the complex conjugate of <math>M_+</math>. To perform a rotation on the complex magnetization vector <math>\mathbf{m}</math> due to an RF pulse with angle <math>\alpha</math> and phase <math>\phi</math>, we first apply a change of basis with <math>S^{-1}</math>, then apply standard cartesian [[rotation matrix|rotation matrices]] <math>R_z(\phi)</math>, <math>R_x(\alpha)</math>,<ref name="l281">{{cite journal | last=Hahn | first=E. L. | title=Spin Echoes | journal=Physical Review | volume=80 | issue=4 | date=1950-11-15 | issn=0031-899X | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.80.580 | pages=580–594 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.80.580 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref> then another change of basis with <math>S</math>:<ref name="n606">{{cite journal | last=Woessner | first=D. E. | title=Effects of Diffusion in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spin-Echo Experiments | journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics | volume=34 | issue=6 | date=1961-06-01 | issn=0021-9606 | doi=10.1063/1.1731821 | pages=2057–2061 | url=https://pubs.aip.org/jcp/article/34/6/2057/80177/Effects-of-Diffusion-in-Nuclear-Magnetic-Resonance | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}

&R_z(\phi)=\begin{bmatrix} \cos \phi & -\sin \phi & 0 \\ \sin \phi & \cos \phi & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\;\;R_x(\alpha)=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & \cos \alpha & -\sin \alpha \\
0 & \sin \alpha & \cos \alpha \end{bmatrix}\\
&\\
&T_\phi (\alpha)=SR_z(\phi)R_x(\alpha)R_z(-\phi)S^{-1}\\
&\\
&T_\phi (\alpha)=\begin{bmatrix} \cos^2 \frac{\alpha}{2} & e^{2i\phi}\sin^2 \frac{\alpha}{2} & -e^{i\phi}\sin \alpha \\
e^{-2i\phi} \sin^2 \frac{\alpha}{2} & \cos^2 \frac{\alpha}{2} & ie^{-i\phi} \sin \alpha\\
-\frac{i}{2}e^{-i\phi} \sin \alpha & \frac{i}{2}e^{i\phi} \sin \alpha & \cos \alpha \end{bmatrix}\\
&\\
&\mathbf{m}^+(z)=T_\phi (\alpha)\mathbf{m}(z)
\end{align}</math>

Where <math>\mathbf{m}^+</math> denotes the magnetization vector after the rotation. In the EPG representation we perform a [[Fourier decomposition]] of each element of the complex magnetization vector:<ref name="hennig"/>

<math display="block">\begin{align}

&M_+(z)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} F_+(k)e^{i2\pi kz} \; \Leftrightarrow \; F_+(k)=\int_{-0.5}^{0.5} M_+(z)e^{-i2\pi kz}dz\\

&M_-(z)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} F_-(k)e^{i2\pi kz} \; \Leftrightarrow \; F_-(k)=\int_{-0.5}^{0.5} M_-(z)e^{-i2\pi kz}dz\\

&M_z(z)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} Z(k)e^{i2\pi kz} \; \Leftrightarrow \; Z(k)=\int_{-0.5}^{0.5} M_z(z)e^{-i2\pi kz}dz\\

\end{align}</math>

If <math>F_+(k)=0</math>, <math>F_-(k)=0</math>, and <math>Z(k)=0</math> when <math>k>n</math> or <math>k<-n</math>. We can write the summations as being from <math>k=-n</math> to <math>n</math>. We can also write the Fourier coefficients as a vector valued function:

<math display="block">\begin{align}

&\mathbf{f}(k)=\begin{bmatrix} F_+(k) \\ F_-(k) \\ Z(k) \end{bmatrix}, &\mathbf{m}(z)=\sum_{k=-n}^{n} \mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz} \\

\end{align}</math>

===RF pulses===

When performing a rotation, because <math>T_\phi (\alpha)</math> is constant across <math>k</math> it can enter the sum:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\mathbf{m}^+(z)=T_\phi (\alpha)\mathbf{m}(z)=\sum_k T_\phi (\alpha)\mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}\\
&\mathbf{f}^+(k)=T_\phi (\alpha)\mathbf{f}(k)
\end{align}</math>

It can be seen in the equation above that the rotation matrix can be applied directly to the Fourier coefficients to produce updated Fourier coefficients.<ref name="pureandsimple">{{cite journal|author1=Matthias Weigel |doi=10.1002/jmri.24619|title=Extended phase graphs: dephasing, RF pulses, and echoes - pure and simple |journal=J Magn Reson Imaging|year=2015}}</ref>

===Gradients===
A gradient in the z dimension that creates one twist from <math>z=-0.5</math> to <math>z=0.5</math> can be applied with the matrix:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&T(z)=SR_z(2\pi z)S^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix} e^{i2\pi z} & 0 & 0\\ 0 & e^{-i2\pi z} & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\\
\end{align}</math>

This matrix is independent of <math>k</math> so it can enter the Fourier sum:<ref name="b176">{{cite journal | last1=Lukzen | first1=N.N. | last2=Savelov | first2=A.A. | title=Analytical derivation of multiple spin echo amplitudes with arbitrary refocusing angle | journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance | volume=185 | issue=1 | date=2007 | doi=10.1016/j.jmr.2006.11.010 | pages=71–76 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1090780706003922 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\mathbf{m}^+(z)=T(z)\mathbf{m}(z)= T(z)\sum_k \mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}=\sum_k T(z)\mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}\\
\end{align}</math>

Looking at each element of <math>\mathbf{m}^+</math>:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&M_+^+(z)=\sum_k e^{i2\pi z}F_+(k)e^{i2\pi kz}=\sum_k F_+(k)e^{i2\pi(k+1)z}\\
&M_-^+(z)=\sum_k e^{-i2\pi z}F_-(k)e^{i2\pi kz}=\sum_k F_-(k)e^{i2\pi(k-1)z}\\
&M_z^+(z)=M_z(z)\\
\end{align}</math>

Performing a substitution with <math>\hat{k}=k+1</math> for the first element we get:

<math display="block">\begin{align}

&M_+^+(z)=\sum_{\hat{k}=-n+1}^{n+1} F_+(\hat{k}-1)e^{i2\pi \hat{k} z}\\

\end{align}</math>

If <math>F_+(n)=0</math> and <math>F_+(-n-1)=0</math> the above summation is equal to:<ref name="hennig_echoes">{{cite journal | last=Hennig | first=Jürgen | title=Echoes—how to generate, recognize, use or avoid them in MR‐imaging sequences. Part I: Fundamental and not so fundamental properties of spin echoes | journal=Concepts in Magnetic Resonance | volume=3 | issue=3 | date=1991 | issn=1043-7347 | doi=10.1002/cmr.1820030302 | pages=125–143 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cmr.1820030302 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}

&M_+^+(z)=\sum_{\hat{k}=-n}^{n} F_+(\hat{k}-1)e^{i2\pi \hat{k} z}\\

\end{align}</math>

and it can be seen that <math>F_+^+(k)=F_+(k-1)</math>. By the same logic <math>F_-^+(k)=F_-(k+1)</math>. So gradients in the EPG formalism simply shift the indices of the Fourier coefficients.<ref name="j399">{{cite journal | last=Zur | first=Yuval | title=An algorithm to calculate the NMR signal of a multi spin-echo sequence with relaxation and spin-diffusion | journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance | volume=171 | issue=1 | date=2004 | doi=10.1016/j.jmr.2004.07.018 | pages=97–106 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1090780704002265 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="pureandsimple"/>

===Relaxation===
The relaxation and recovery matrices given by the Bloch equations for a real valued magnetization vector <math>\mathbf{v}</math> are:<ref name="jaynes"/>
<math display="block">\begin{align}

&E=\begin{bmatrix}
e^{-t/T2} & 0 & 0 \\
0 & e^{-t/T2} & 0\\
0 & 0 & e^{-t/T1}\end{bmatrix}, &\mathbf{r}=\begin{bmatrix}
0\\
0\\
M_0(1-e^{-t/T1}) \end{bmatrix}\\
&\\
&\mathbf{v}^+=E\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{r}
\end{align}</math>

Substituting with <math>\mathbf{v}=S^{-1}\mathbf{m}</math>:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&S^{-1}\mathbf{m}^{+}=ES^{-1}\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{r}\\
&\mathbf{m}^{+}=SES^{-1}\mathbf{m}+S\mathbf{r}
\end{align}</math>

<math>S</math> and <math>E</math> are commutative so <math>SES^{-1}=ESS^{-1}=E</math>. Also <math>S\mathbf{r}=\mathbf{r}</math>, so:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\mathbf{m}^{+}(z)=E\mathbf{m}(z)+\mathbf{r}=E \sum_k \mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}+\mathbf{r}=\sum_k E\mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}+\mathbf{r}\\
\end{align}</math>

<math>\mathbf{r}</math> is a constant vector but we can still Fourier decompose it to <math>\mathbf{r}(z)=\sum_k \mathbf{g}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}</math> where <math>\mathbf{g}(k)=\mathbf{r}</math> if <math>\mathbf{k}=0</math> else <math>\mathbf{g}(k)=\mathbf{0}</math>, so:<ref name="pictoral">{{cite journal | last=Scheffler | first=Klaus | title=A pictorial description of steady-states in rapid magnetic resonance imaging | journal=Concepts in Magnetic Resonance | volume=11 | issue=5 | date=1999 | issn=1043-7347 | doi=10.1002/(SICI)1099-0534(1999)11:5<291::AID-CMR2>3.0.CO;2-J | pages=291–304 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/(SICI)1099-0534(1999)11:53.0.CO;2-J | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&\mathbf{m}^{+}(z)=\sum_k E\mathbf{f}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}+\sum_k \mathbf{g}(k)e^{i2\pi kz}=\sum_k (E\mathbf{f}(k)+\mathbf{g}(k))e^{i2\pi kz}\\
\end{align}</math>

So it can be seen that to apply a relaxation, you can multiply every Fourier coefficient with the relaxation matrix <math>E</math> and then add the recovery vector <math>\mathbf{r}</math> to the 0th coefficient.<ref name="schwenk">{{cite journal | last1=Weigel | first1=M. | last2=Schwenk | first2=S. | last3=Kiselev | first3=V.G. | last4=Scheffler | first4=K. | last5=Hennig | first5=J. | title=Extended phase graphs with anisotropic diffusion | journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance | volume=205 | issue=2 | date=2010 | doi=10.1016/j.jmr.2010.05.011 | pages=276–285 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1090780710001540 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Total signal in voxel===
The total transverse signal in the voxel is obtained by integrating over <math>M_+(z)</math>:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&M_{+total}=\int_{-0.5}^{0.5} \sum_{k=-n}^{n} F_+(k)e^{i2\pi kz}\;dz=\sum_{k=-n}^{n} (F_+(k)\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}e^{i2\pi kz}dz)=\sum_{k=-n}^{n} F_+(k)\frac{1}{i2\pi k}(e^{i\pi k}-e^{-i\pi k})\\
\end{align}
</math>

so when <math>k</math> is nonzero, <math>F_+(k)</math> is multiplied by zero and doesn't end up in the sum. If <math>k=0</math> the inner integral is 1. So the total transverse signal in the voxel is just <math>F_+(0)</math>. By the same logic the total longitudinal signal is <math>Z(0)</math>.<ref name="hennig_echoes"/>

===Coefficient redundancy===
It can be proven that <math>F_+(k)=F_-(-k)^*</math>:<ref name="pictoral"/><ref name="d401">{{cite journal | last=Sodickson | first=A | title=A generalized k-space formalism for treating the spatial aspects of a variety of NMR experiments | journal=Progress in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy | volume=33 | issue=2 | date=1998-08-31 | doi=10.1016/S0079-6565(98)00021-1 | pages=77–108 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0079656598000211 | access-date=2026-01-25| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
&F_-(k)=\int M_+(z)^*e^{-i2\pi kz}dz\\
&F_-(-k)=\int M_+(z)^*e^{i2\pi kz}dz=\int (M_+(z)e^{-i2\pi kz})^*dz=F_+(k)^*\\
\end{align}</math>

and so in practice only coefficients with <math>k\ge 0</math> are stored and if a gradient occurs that would shift a coefficient to having a negative index, instead that coefficient is conjugated and stored at a non-negative index.

==Computation==
In practice, a discrete number of Fourier coefficients are tracked. A matrix can be set up with <math>n+1</math> frequencies tracked like so:<ref name="schwenk"/>

<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
F_+(0) & F_+(1) & ... & F_+(n)\\
F_-(0) & F_-(1) & ... & F_-(n)\\
Z(0) & Z(1) & ... & Z(n)\\ \end{bmatrix}
</math>

This matrix can be multiplied by the RF pulse rotation matrix <math>T_\phi (\alpha)</math>, or multiplied by the relaxation matrix <math>E</math> and then have <math>\textbf{r}</math> added to the first column, to update the coefficients. A gradient that adds one twist along the z dimension will result in the first row being shifted right by one, and the second row being shifted left. Then <math>F_+(0)</math> can be set to <math>F_-(0)^*</math>.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Hargreaves |first1=Brian |last2=Miller |first2=Karla |date=2013 |title=Using extended phase graphs: review and examples. |url=https://archive.ismrm.org/2013/3718.html| conference=Proceedings of the 21st Annual Meeting of ISMRM |location=Salt Lake City}}</ref>
